title: Query optimisation: plan-space example
lead: The Reserves/Sailors example from the source slides, with the same data sizes and cost assumptions.

sections.title: Source query and selection pushdown
sections.html:
The source uses Reserves with 1000 pages and 100 tuples/page, Sailors with 500 pages and 80 tuples/page, 100 equally likely boat IDs, 10 equally likely ratings and B = 5 join buffers. The query returns sname where R.sid = S.sid, R.bid = 100 and S.rating > 5.

Page nested loops with Sailors outside costs 500 + 500·1000 = 500,500 I/Os. Filtering the outer input reduces its packed output to 250 page-equivalents, giving 500 + 250·1000 = 250,500.

Filtering the inner Reserves scan on the fly still reads all 1000 source pages on each rescan. It reduces output tuples but does not reduce that scan’s page reads. The estimates use the slides’ packed-stream accounting.

PDF pp. 1–13

sections.title: Join order and materialisation
sections.html:
Move filtered Reserves to the outer input. The first scan costs 1000; its 1/100 fraction produces 10 page-equivalents. Ten Sailors rescans cost 10·500, giving 6000 I/Os.

Materialising filtered Sailors first costs a 500-page scan and 250 writes. Joining against those 250 temporary pages costs 1000 + 500 + 250 + 10·250 = 4250.

Reversing the orientation and materialising the 10-page Reserves result costs 500 + 1000 + 10 + 250·10 = 4010. A temporary relation incurs its write once and its read on every rescan; neither should be silently omitted.

PDF pp. 14–24

sections.title: Join algorithms and narrower tuples
sections.html:
With B = 5, sorting the filtered 10-page Reserves stream requires two passes and the 250-page Sailors stream four. The source counts base scans once, initial sort writes, later sort reads/writes and a final merge: 1500 + 30 + 1750 + 260 = 3540 I/Os.

Block nested loops uses three outer frames. Streaming filtered Sailors against materialised Reserves costs 500 + 1000 + 10 + ⌈250/3⌉·10 = 2350.

Projecting filtered Reserves to its 4-byte sid reduces its 10 pages of 40-byte tuples to one page under the source packing assumptions. Keeping that outer input in memory permits one scan of each base relation: 1000 + 500 = 1500 I/Os.

PDF pp. 25–38

sections.title: Indexed plan and comparison
sections.html:
The final plan assumes a clustered tree index on Reserves.bid, an unclustered tree index on Sailors.sid and index navigation already in memory. The bid predicate retrieves 1000 Reserves tuples on 10 data pages.

For each tuple, the sid index finds at most one Sailors record because sid is a key. At one data-page I/O per match, the estimate is 10 + 1000·1 = 1010 I/Os. Filtering rating afterwards does not remove the need to fetch that Sailors tuple.

The sequence is 500,500 → 250,500 → 6000 → 4250 → 4010 → 3540 → 2350 → 1500 → 1010. These are estimates for the source’s alternatives, not measurements or a proof that no other plan is cheaper.

PDF pp. 39–43

quiz.question: Does filtering an inner heap from 600 pages to 12 output pages automatically reduce each scan to 12 I/Os?
options: No, if each scan still reads the 600-page heap
It depends only on the number of SELECT columns
quiz.explanation: Output size and the number of input pages that must be read are different quantities.

source.summary: The full official PDF has been reviewed. Coverage includes repeated plan refinement; selection pushdown inside and outside nested loops; join orientation; materializing filtered inner input; sort-merge pass accounting; block nested loops and projection width; and clustered outer access with an indexed inner join. The explanations and calculations are original teaching material rather than reproductions of the slides.

topics: Clustered outer lookup and indexed inner join
